title: The 25 Best Left Wingers in World Soccer—Ranked
subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By SI FC StaffAug 19, 2025Khvicha Kvaratskhelia is universally adored, and rightly so. / Image Photo Agency/Getty ImagesSoccer used to be simple. Wingers hugged the touchline, beat their man and whipped crosses in for a towering striker to nod home.

Left wingers have taken many forms over the years—from the graceful flair of Brazilian artists to the no-nonsense directness of English wide men. And in the modern game, that diversity has only grown. Today, a winger’s role is shaped entirely by the system they play in—inside forwards, inverted creators, traditional touchline stretchers. It all depends on the context.

Being a left winger now is anything but straightforward. Yet despite the tactical complexity, their mission remains familiar: excite, create and make a difference. And right now, the position is stacked with elite-level talent.
Here’s Sports Illustrated’s ranking of the best in the business right now.

Kaoru Mitoma is a dribbling fiend for Brighton. / Clive Rose/Getty ImagesThe dribbling theorist has studied his way to soccer stardom. His university work undoubtedly played a huge role in his easy-on-the-eye style, with Kaoru Mitoma emerging as a one-on-one phenom since joining Brighton in 2021.The Japan international eventually starred for the Seagulls after returning from a loan in Belgium and is seen as the next Brighton star who’ll garner a monster fee when he decides to take the next step. A long list of clubs have been queuing up to sign him for years.

Alberto Moleiro is diminutive but impressive. / Pedro Salado/Getty ImagesA Spain U-21 international unhelpfully burdened with the tag of becoming the ‘new Pedri’ has instead established himself in his own name. Alberto Moleiro has thrived as the creative fulcrum of Villarreal’s impressive attack, constantly drifting off his perch on the left flank to wreak havoc between the stitching of opponents’ rearguards.Given Pedri’s well-documented struggles to consistently provide goals and assists, Moleiro’s impressive record in that regard could perhaps offer an inspiration for the Barcelona midfielder.

Gabriel Martinelli now finds himself at Al Hilal. / Abdullah Ahmed/Getty ImagesGabriel Martinelli’s journey at Arsenal did, in many ways, exceed expectations. Plucked from relative obscurity at Brazilian side Ituano, he's carved out a regular role in a top Premier League side—bringing pace, unpredictability and a relentless drive down the left flank.At the same time, there will always be a lingering sense of unfulfilled potential. One standout season hinted at a breakout star, but inconsistency held him back. Too often, flashes of brilliance were followed by stretches of quiet performances. Martinelli was restricted to the role of super sub while the Gunners ended their long wait for a Premier League title.Mikel Arteta ultimately cashed in on a winger who still has the dangerous weapons of raw speed and energy, which the rest of the Saudi Pro League are still getting used to.

Serge Gnabry remains a prolific presence for Bayern Munich. / S. Stingl/FC Bayern/Getty ImagesSerge Gnabry may be edging toward the latter stages of his career, and his output has dipped in recent seasons, but don’t be fooled, he remains an extremely versatile, technically gifted forward who can still deliver on the biggest stage with Bayern Munich.A strong finisher off both feet with sharp movement and clever positioning, Gnabry has always possessed a striker’s instinct. He consistently pops up in the right place at the right time, making late runs into the box and finishing with precision. Even if he’s no longer the explosive force of a few years ago, he’s still a major threat in the final third—capable of turning tight matches with a goal or a moment of decisive quality.

Nico Williams could leave Athletic Club. / Alcoba Beitia/Getty ImagesNico Williams is pure chaos on the wing—all pace, power and that fearless, straight-at-you style that defenders hate to deal with.He’s direct, dangerous, and technically razor-sharp. The kind of winger who’s already got you panicking before the ball even reaches his feet. And unlike so many modern wide men coached to play it safe, Williams doesn’t hesitate—he wants to beat you. Over and over again.Already a star for Athletic Club, he carried that same energy into Euro 2024, scoring in the final as Spain lifted the trophy. Injury limited his involvement at the 2026 World Cup, but it was Williams’s introduction which gave La Roja the jolt to find a way past Argentina in the final, nodding the ball back for Ferran Torres’s famous winner.Having snubbed Spanish giants Barcelona to commit his long-term future to Bilbao, it’s exciting to think just how far he can help carry the club in the years ahead.

Ademola Lookman made the move to Atlético Madrid in January. / Joaquin Corchero/Europa Press/Getty ImagesAdemola Lookman’s early career—hopping from Everton to RB Leipzig, then back through loan spells at Fulham and Leicester—felt like a talent in limbo. He was miscast, misunderstood and too often overlooked. So when he was crowned 2024 African Footballer of the Year and placed 14th in the Ballon d’Or rankings, the hesitation from some corners of the soccer world said more about old biases than it did about his ability.Because let’s be clear: Lookman is the real deal. At Atalanta, the Nigerian international flourished. Whether drifting wide or operating in the half-spaces, he became a constant menace—blending pace, precision and intelligence with a ruthless streak in front of goal. A historic Europa League final hat-trick was the peak.Things soured towards the end of his time in Bergamo but Lookman is playing with the same punch Atlético Madrid after a switch at the start of 2026.

Antonio Nusa is a wonderfully gifted talent. / Stuart Franklin/Getty ImagesIn a Norway side dominated by the figures of Erling Haaland and Martin Ødegaard, it is Antonio Nusa who most regularly gets the Nordic crowd off their feet.The creative trickster honed his skills thanks to hours spent pouring over footage of his idol. “I watched clips of Neymar on YouTube and went out to try to copy him,” Nusa bluntly explained when quizzed on how he developed his array of gifts.After years of out-performing his club form at international level, RB Leipzig are finally enjoying the most productive version of Nusa. With a host of Europe’s watching on admiration, it’s not clear how much longer that will remain the case.

Rio Ngumoha is not your normal teenager. / Marc Atkins/Getty ImagesRio Ngumoha’s talent has been clear for years—and he still won’t be able to buy alcohol in the States until 2029. The former Chelsea academy gem who was poached by Liverpool has already made a mockery of the modest $9 million an independent tribunal ordered the Merseyside club pay their London counterparts. No wonder Chelsea want more.Bursting with an infectious zeal to run at, around or behind whatever opponent is unfortunately enough to be faced with his dancing feet, Ngumoha’s talent is prodigious. The senior England international has plenty more room for growth as it is, rounding out his game by moonlighting on the right wing following Mohamed Salah’s Liverpool exit.

Said El Mala is a German soccer gem. / Osama Faisal/SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesGerman soccer has been through somewhat of a malaise, particularly since their 2014 World Cup triumph. But a new generation, led by Jürgen Klopp, is hoping to banish the memories of a difficult decade—and Said El Mala is already playing his part for the national team.Another pacy, direct attacker who isn’t afraid to take the game to opposition defenders, El Mala has all the attributes required to be a successful modern day winger. It’s no surprise that he’s quickly established himself as one of the Bundesliga’s brightest young gems, registering a glut of goals for 1. FC Köln as they aim to re-establish themselves as a solid top-flight club.El Mala’s talent also runs in the family—his father played as a center back and his older brother, Malek, is also a forward on the books of 1. FC Köln.

Iliman Ndiaye has come a long way in a short time. / Marc Atkins/Getty ImagesIliman Nidaye is one of soccer’s feel-good stories. As recently as 2019, the French-born forward was playing non-League. Within three years, he had represented Senegal at the World Cup.The rubbery winger would go to his second global jamboree in 2026, a few weeks before becoming the most expensive player in the history his nation when joining Manchester City. “Giving up is not in my dictionary,” the affable forward would beam years after turning out for Boreham Wood. “I’ve always believed that one day I’m going to be the best player in the world and that’s what keeps me going.”

Rafael Leão made the move to Galatasaray in 2026. / Arif Hudaverdi Yaman/Anadolu/Getty ImagesOn his day, Rafael Leão might just be the most devastating winger on the planet. Give him a loose ball, and he doesn’t hesitate—accelerating with terrifying speed, shrugging off challenges like they’re nothing and charging directly at goal with the kind of conviction defenders dread. There are few players in world soccer who can carry the ball with such raw, destructive intent.At his best, he’s unplayable, but that version of Leão doesn’t always show up. Since helping AC Milan to a long-awaited Scudetto in 2022–23, his form has fluctuated wildly. One game he looks like a Ballon d’Or contender, the next he's barely involved.With that backdrop, it’s fitting that Leão has taken his talents to Türkiye, where he can try and save the best of his mercurial form for the Champions League.

Alex Baena is a World Cup winner. / Javier Borrego/Europa Press/Getty ImagesAlex Baena is the perfect tool for club and country. Boasting the grit and gristle which Diego Simeone so favors, Atlético Madrid’s World Cup winner is pivotal to Luis de la Fuente’s international exploits.Dancing the fine line between attacking midfielder and winger, Baena is a selfless creator who overcame homesickness to blossom at Villarreal. After some teething problems during his debut season in the Spanish capital, Atlético are seeing the best of Baena in his second campaign.

Kenan Yıldız is Juve’s star man. / Daniele Badolato/Juventus FC/Getty ImagesBetween Arda Güler and Kenan Yıldız, Turkey’s future isn’t just bright—it’s on fire.Where Güler brings poise and playmaking flair, Yıldız is his chaos-fuelled counterpart: all power, pace, and pure instinct. A fearless dribbler and explosive striker of the ball, the Juventus youngster has quickly built a reputation as a walking highlight reel.In what was otherwise a forgettable 2025–26 season for Juve, the youngster stood out as a rare beacon of excitement—racking up 11 goals and nine assists across all competitions. And these weren’t tap-ins either. Many were long-range rockets, hit with the kind of swagger and venom you can’t teach.Sure, he's still ironing out the consistency, but the raw talent is unmistakable. Once the polish catches up to the potential, Yıldız will be one of Europe’s most dangerous attacking forces, and Turkey will have their next superstar.

Karim Adeyemi is rapid. / BERK OZKAN/AFP/Getty ImagesKarim Adeyemi’s lightning pace might be the first thing you notice—and with good reason. The German winger is among the fastest players in world soccer, using his jet-fuelled acceleration to leave defenders gasping for air.But there’s more to his game than raw speed. At Borussia Dortmund, he began to refine the chaos—developing sharper movement, better decision-making and a growing calmness in front of goal. Barcelona were convinced to whisk him away to Catalonia, where all the pieces seem to be falling into place.It’s proof that Adeyemi isn’t just a blur on the flank anymore. He’s evolving into a well-rounded, high-impact attacker.
